acceptedAnswer.text: It is ambiguous as written — by the common convention this calculator uses, trailing zeros with no decimal point are not significant, so "100" reads as 1 sig fig. Writing 100. (with a trailing decimal point) or 1.00 × 10² removes the ambiguity and gives 3 sig figs.

mainEntity.name: Are exact numbers and defined constants exempt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Counting numbers (12 eggs) and exactly defined conversion factors (100 cm = 1 m, by definition) have effectively infinite significant figures and never limit the precision of a calculation.

Always rounding a trailing 5 up introduces a small systematic bias over many roundings. Rounding to the nearest even digit instead splits ties evenly between rounding up and down, keeping large-sample averages unbiased.

mainEntity.name: How are significant figures different from decimal places?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decimal places count digits after the decimal point regardless of where they start; significant figures count meaningful digits starting from the first non-zero digit. 0.002 has 3 decimal places but only 1 significant figure.
Scientific notation removes all ambiguity: every digit in the mantissa (the part before ×10ⁿ) is significant by convention, since no digit is needed purely to place the decimal point.

mainEntity.name: Does the sig-fig rule apply the same way to subtraction as addition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — subtraction follows the same decimal-places rule as addition. Note that subtracting two close, imprecise numbers can dramatically reduce the number of significant figures in the result (called "catastrophic cancellation").
